newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany seen launching pension funds in Feb 1998.
newsitem.headline: Germany seen launching pension funds in Feb 1998.

text.p: Germany is likely to approve the launch of its first pension funds in February next year, according to Rolf Passow, chief executive of the German association of investment companies.
Launching the funds would form part of widely debated changes to the German pensions system, currently a government-run pay-as-you-go system.

Passow told the Frankfurt journalists' club on Tuesday evening that the association was working with Germany's federal banking supervisory authority to draw up model contracts for the regulatory approval of about 100 special pension funds.

Such funds will be legally allowed for the first time under the so-called "Third Law" to promote German financial markets, which is due for discussion in the German cabinet soon. The law is generally expected to be passed without major revisions.

The funds, which are intended to be a mainstay of firms' pension support, are expected to invest mainly in equities, potentially giving a further boost German share market prices, currently at record levels.

Passow said the surge in the share market -- which has gained over 40 percent so far this year -- had brought over 50 million marks ($27.9 million) in new funds into German capital investment funds and their overseas subsidiaries.
About 70 percent of this had gone into shares, compared with a more usual level of about 20 to 25 percent.
"If we could keep this level at about 40 percent for the next 10 years it would be an excellent result," Passow said.
German-based investment funds and their subsidiaries currently managed over 910 billion marks of funds, he added. The total would exceed a trillion by the year 2000.
Passow strongly opposed government moves to tax speculative gains by investment funds from sales of shares held for less than 12 months. The so-called speculation period is currently six months.
